extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of 19th-century travel/literary essays (readers of Irving's Sketch Book)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing descriptive, anecdotal travel or country-life essays in a Romantic/early-19th-century literary mode that record customs, moralize, and include illustrative tales. Emphasis on picturesque detail, moral reflection, and anecdotal storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strewing flowers at funerals / grave decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom of strewing flowers before funerals and planting them at graves — an ancient, simple-hearted rural practice observed in England and other countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as spontaneous tributes of affection (Greeks, Romans, rural England); examples and poetic quotations (Ophelia, Herrick, Shakespeare) are used to illustrate the practice. Notes that the custom now survives chiefly in remote villages and is renewed seasonally; contrast made with costly monuments of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaplets of white flowers for young unmarried females
rubrics_metrics.description: A chaplet of white flowers is borne before the corpse by a young girl nearest in age, size, and resemblance and afterwards hung in the church over the deceased's accustomed seat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaplets sometimes made of white paper and contain a pair of white gloves; intended as emblems of purity and the crown of glory received in heaven. Example given as a distinct rite for young, unmarried women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of flowers, ribbons, and colors as emblematic language
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and color of flowers and of the ribbons with which they were tied often referenced the qualities or story of the deceased or expressed the mourner's feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific emblematic uses cited: white rose for a virgin (spotless innocence), red rose for benevolence, roses generally for lovers; black and yellow ribbons mentioned in an old poem; ribbons sometimes intermingled (white with black) to show purity plus grief. Poetic passages illustrate these symbolic pairings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy emblems for disappointed lovers (yew, cypress)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the deceased had been unhappy in love, more gloomy emblems such as the yew and cypress were used and, if flowers were strewn, they were of melancholy colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported with poetic citations (e.g., 'Yet strew / Upon my dismall grave... forsaken cypresse and yewe') and ballad fragments (e.g., 'Lay a garland on my hearse / Of the dismall yew'). This governs choice of plant-material according to life story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for sweet-scented evergreens and flowers
rubrics_metrics.description: It was an especial precaution that none but sweet-scented evergreens and flowers should be employed in funeral decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to soften the horrors of the tomb and associate the memory of the deceased with delicate natural objects; cited as a general principle underlying the tasteful arrangement of funeral offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, spontaneous rural offerings preferred over costly monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Spontaneous floral offerings (the hand strewing a flower while the heart is warm) are morally and aesthetically superior to costly, sculptured monuments and hireling displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: pathos expires under slow chisel-work; rural, immediate tributes preserve genuine feeling, while urban funerals become 'show and gloomy parade' with mourning carriages, plumes, and hireling mourners that make a mockery of grief. Encourages simplicity, sincerity, and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearest relatives perform rites; no hirelings or paid mourners
rubrics_metrics.description: Funeral strewing and planting is 'invariably performed by the nearest relatives and friends; no menials nor hirelings are employed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a neighbor helps, offering compensation would be an insult. This prescribes who should do the rites and prohibits commercialization of mourning in the rural custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal of floral tributes on religious festivals
rubrics_metrics.description: Where strewing and planting survives, it is renewed on Easter, Whitsuntide, and other festivals when the season revives the flowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal practice ties commemoration to the church calendar and recurring communal remembrance; cited as part of the custom's persistence and social rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traveler's conduct toward passing funerals
rubrics_metrics.description: A traveller encountering a rural funeral should pause uncovered, let it pass, and often follow silently in the rear for some distance as a mark of respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavior is described as a solemn respect paid by travellers; sometimes they follow to the grave and then resume their journey. It is an etiquette for the passer-by in rural communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect graves and plant evergreens/osiers to preserve turf
rubrics_metrics.description: Graves were once protected with bent osiers, and evergreens (holly, rosemary, etc.) were planted about them to keep the turf uninjured and commemorate the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given of holly and rosemary grown luxuriantly to overshadow tombstones; practice contrasted with mere strewing that withers quickly—planting gives permanence and living memorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral ornamentation often encodes personal narrative or virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of garlands and the choice of sundry-colored flowers or ribbons can be deliberately arranged 'in token of good-will' or to narrate the qualities of the deceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the poem 'Corydon’s Doleful Knell' where a lover specifies garland colors and ribbons, promising to 'deck her tomb with flowers / The rarest ever seen'—shows how decoration functions semiotically to tell a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling effectiveness depends on manner and narrator's presence
rubrics_metrics.description: The zest of a traveller's anecdote often derives chiefly from the manner in which it is told and the peculiar air and appearance of the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's observation from the inn kitchen: many tales are dull in content, but the delivery (voice, gestures, persona) and the setting (stove, company) transform them; implies that a good anecdote requires performance as much as material.
